I turn 18 today. 70 days ago, I moved to SF. No friends. No experience. Just graduated high school. Here's what I learned: -> 1. Cold DM I cold messaged Chungin Lee in April after Cluely went viral. Didn't expect a response at all. Received an offer a week later. Cold messaged founders on X. Landed my internship at General Translation with 4 Princeton grads. -> 2. Be high agency My friend and I snuck into ThirdLayer (YC W25) office at 4 AM. He pitched his startup to the founders while washing their dishes. In 15 minutes, he booked a call, gained a research opportunity & left a lasting impression. -> 3. Have audacity I walked up to someone wearing a Browserbase hoodie. Asked for merch because I liked their product. Ended up in their office, met their entire team & founder. In the past 18 years, I’ve learned the most in these 70 days. So if you're young and thinking about leaping: Do it. Send the DM Ask for the meeting. Show up anyway. The worst they can say is no. Usually they say yes. ...more

Last week I was flown out to Los Angeles by Hack Club for a 3-day hackathon called Ascend that I helped organize for girls in tech! For the past few months, my team and I have been working hard to make this hackathon unforgettable. From venue searching to coordinating flights for attendees (it was all expenses paid for!), it was magical to see our hundreds of hours of work come to life. Our attendees got the chance of a lifetime—an exclusive tour of SpaceX headquarters! It was inspiring to see all the SpaceX engineers in action right in front of me. The highlight was definitely seeing actual Falcon rockets and spacecraft components. After the tour, our attendees got to network and receive project mentorship from actual SpaceX engineers! We wrapped up our final day with a special breakfast featuring SpaceX engineers and other tech leaders from the Los Angeles area like Yen Tan , the co-founder of Kona and Daria Shapovalova the founder of DressX. The most surreal moment was meeting Maria Liberman and David and Daniil Liberman , the creators of Snapchat AR since I had learned about their work a few years prior. A massive thank you to the SpaceX engineers like Caila Shannon , Carissa Bailey , Sarah Ting , Asher Dunn , and many others for opening their doors and minds to the next generation of engineers. I also can’t thank Zenab Hassan , Zach Latta , and Christina Asquith enough for overseeing this hackathon and giving me the opportunity to organize it. Lastly, to the incredible Ascend organizing team: thank you for being my best friends and the most supportive team. ...more

YC scores every startup on a 100-point scale. 70 of those points come from just one thing. Last month we took our first BridgeFellows cohort to Y Combinator headquarters in San Francisco. Our fellows pitched and got grilled by Grey Baker (General Partner at YC) and Finbarr Taylor (Visiting Partner at YC). Afterwards, Grey walked us through the mental model YC uses to evaluate founders. Not their literal scoring system, but how they think about it. Imagine 100 points available. The pass mark for getting into YC and its $500K check is about 65. → Team: ~70 points. The strongest predictor of whether you'll build something big. Founders pivot, but the team stays. If they're exceptional, the eventual idea usually is too. → Idea / space: ~20 points. Being in a plausible space matters because it's where your team can actually find something big to build. → Traction: ~10 points on its own. Not required. But if you have real traction, it lifts your team and idea scores too. Most founders think you need revenue to get into YC. You don't. 70% of the current YC batch (W26) had $0 in revenue when they got in. Traction is not what gets you in. Team is. The best example Grey gave was Brex. Two 19-year-olds walked into YC with cardboard VR glasses you clip your phone into. Bad idea. No traction. Funded anyway. Why? At 16, they'd built and sold a company for $100M. Clearly exceptional founders. They pivoted early in the batch to what became Brex. Today it's worth billions. The idea you apply with is usually not the idea you build. That's exactly why they bet on the team. Thanks to Grey and Finbarr for taking the time with our fellows.

I’m excited to share a project that my sister, Isabel, and I have been working on for the past few months: Stories We Inherit: History Through Their Eyes, a podcast that we co-host, exploring the stories, experiences, and history passed down through generations. Our first episode is officially live on Spotify. In this episode, we share the stories of our grandparents growing up in China during the Great Famine and Cultural Revolution, and explore what it meant to come of age during such a turbulent period in Chinese history. As we worked on this episode, we realized how many stories like theirs are rarely heard outside of the families who carry them. We hope Stories We Inherit can grow beyond our own family and become a space for people to share the experiences, memories, and histories that shaped their lives. This project has been a much bigger undertaking than we initially expected. It started as the final project in an elective called Talk To Me: Radio and Podcasting, taught by Professor Judith Sloan, but it quickly spiraled as we realized the depth and significance of our grandparents’ stories. From researching and writing the episode to recording, editing, producing the music, talking to my grandparents, working with voice actors, and figuring out podcast distribution, we built the entire thing from the ground up. More than anything, I’m excited that these stories are no longer sitting in our family conversations. They’re now out in the world. And we want to hear yours. If you have a family story, personal experience, or piece of history you think deserves to be heard, we’d love to hear from you. Reach us at storiesweinherit@gmail.com . Listen to Episode 1: https://lnkd.in/exWFZWwE And a huge thank you to everyone who helped bring this episode to life, especially our voice actors Rocco Romano and Angelina Wang.

This past week, I wrapped up my internship at Pacxa and Tradewind Group , and I’m incredibly grateful for everything I learned over the past two months. As an AI Engineering Intern, I was immersed in building and deploying AI-powered features for Pacxa’s Huaka‘i portal, a new talent marketplace. My work ranged from developing an AI Resume Coach and job-posting assistant to building the data infrastructure that supports them. Along the way, I gained hands-on experience working with Azure AI Foundry, developing full-stack applications, and designing reliable systems around large language models. I want to thank my mentors Amberlene M. Thompson, CSM® , Kai Sunahara , Haley Benn , and Jodi Yamane for their guidance throughout the summer; Alec Kimura for leading the internship program; and my fellow interns for making the experience both collaborative and enjoyable. I’m also grateful to Kelly J. Ueoka and everyone else at Pacxa who took the time to share their knowledge with me. As I move forward, I’m excited to pursue new opportunities in technology where I can apply what I’ve learned and continue to grow!
